title: Stop Throwing Away Hard Loaves: How to Revive Stale Bread Perfectly
description: Learn how to revive stale bread into a crusty, warm loaf that tastes fresh from a French bakery using this simple, foolproof kitchen trick.
story: It was pouring rain outside my tiny apartment window, and I was halfway through making a cozy pot of tomato soup when I realized my artisanal sourdough from Trader Joe's felt like an actual brick. Honestly, I almost tossed it straight into the trash. But wasting food always breaks my heart, so I remembered this old trick. I ran the crust under the kitchen faucet, popped it straight into a hot oven, and prayed. Ten minutes later, my entire kitchen smelled like a Parisian patisserie. The crust shattered with that perfect crackle, and the inside turned wonderfully soft and chewy again. It honestly saved dinner.
ingredients: 1 stale loaf of crusty bread (sourdough, baguette, or Italian batard)
Cold tap water (just enough to wet the crust thoroughly)
2 tablespoons Kerrygold unsalted butter (optional, for brushing)
1 pinch of flaky sea salt (like Maldon)
1 clove garlic, halved (optional, for rubbing post-bake)
instructions: Step 1: Run your stale loaf of bread directly under the cold kitchen tap, making sure the entire outer crust is thoroughly soaked. Don't be shy with the water, but try not to let it soak deep into the crumb.
Step 2: Place the wet loaf directly onto the center oven rack. No baking sheet needed! Heating it directly on the metal promotes an even, crispy crust.
Step 3: Bake in a preheated oven at 425 degrees Fahrenheit for 8 to 12 minutes. The water on the crust turns to steam, rehydrating the inside while the dry heat crisps the outside.
Step 4: Remove it from the oven, listen for that satisfying hollow crackle when you tap it, and slice while warm.
proHack: The first time I tried this, I wrapped the loaf in foil and ended up with soggy mush instead of a crust—always bake it completely naked on the rack so the steam can escape and crisp up the exterior!
storage: If you somehow have leftovers, let the bread cool completely, then store it in a paper bag on the counter for up to one day. Avoid plastic bags, which trap moisture and ruin the crust.

faqs.question: Can I use this method for pre-sliced sandwich bread?
faqs.answer: No, this trick works best for whole, crusty artisan loaves like baguettes, sourdough, or ciabatta. Sliced sandwich bread will just get soggy and weird.

faqs.question: How do I prevent the bread from burning in the oven?
faqs.answer: Keep a close eye on it during the last three minutes. If your oven runs hot, drop the temperature down to 400 degrees Fahrenheit so the crust doesn't char before the inside warms through.
